newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Izetbegovic beats Serb in Bosnian presidency race.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic beats Serb in Bosnian presidency race.

text.p: The man who led Bosnia through war, Alija Izetbetovic, narrowly defeated one of his Serb nationalist foes to become the head of a peacetime collective presidency, election organisers said on Wednesday.
The outcome was greeted with relief by Western governments because Izetbegovic, a Moslem, wants to reunify the country.
His main challenger for the presidency chair, Serb hardliner Momcilo Krajisnik is a separatist whose party ripped apart Bosnia in war and waged a pro-secession campaign.
But Bosnia's main Moslem party has turned increasingly nationalist, inviting obstruction by Serb and Croat separatists and complicating efforts to unite the three in government.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which supervised the September 14 elections, said a completed count gave Izetbegovic 724,199 votes, and Krajisnik 690,373.
The third and final seat on the joint executive went to Bosnian Croat nationalist Kresimir Zubak who took 294,300 votes. All results were unofficial pending certification.
"It appears clear that President Izetbegovic will serve as the new president of the presidency," said Robert Frowick, head of the OSCE mission in Bosnia.

The result means Izetbegovic will be effective head of state for the next two years, a period pivotal for moves to reconcile Moslem, Serb and Croat-dominated sectors of Bosnia under the 1995 Dayton treaty that ended 43 months of war.
But the presidency must govern by consensus, a formula that could, without fulltime Western diplomatic engagement, cause the kind of nationalist standoffs that degenerated into war.

Apart from voting for the country's joint presidency, Bosnians were asked to choose representatives in five other assemblies: a multi-ethnic national parliament, a president and parliament for the Serb Republic, a parliament for the Moslem Croat Federation, and Federation Cantonal assemblies.
Voting results still filtering in showed the three main ethnic nationalist parties were comfortably ahead in each of the polls.

In the ballot for the country's joint 42-member House of Representatives, the Moslem Party of Democratic Action (SDA) was emerging as the dominant party. Bosnian Moslems account for more than 40 percent of the population.

Early results indicated Serb nationalists would control the Serb republic's National Assembly but may find themselves sharing the chamber with some of their Moslem rivals who snatched over 6 percent of the vote with the help of refugees.

Biljana Plavsic of the SDS appeared headed for victory in the race for the Serb Republic presidency, winning about 66 percent of the vote. Plavsic is currently acting Bosnian Serb president after international pressure forced indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic to step down.
In the Federation Assembly race, the SDA and the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) were comfortably ahead.
With the major nationalist parties and their leaders prevailing, analysts said the post-war parliament and presidency could soon become paralysed.
Through the war, Momcilo Krajisnik earned a reputation as an extreme nationalist who refuses to compromise.
But Western diplomats say they expect him to cooperate -- at least initially -- in new power-sharing arrangements to stave off threats of indefinite U.N. sanctions.
The one surprise in the presidency polling was the robust showing of a little-known Serb opposition figure who advocated cooperation and compromise with Bosnia's Moslem and Croat communities.
Mladen Ivanic took almost a third of Serb votes -- a result that a spokesman for international peace coordinator Carl Bildt touted as "the beginnings of pluralism" in the Serb Republic.

Some analysts said Ivanic's performace confirmed a growing backlash against ultra-nationalists in Krajisnik's SDS, who laid siege to Sarajevo and grew fat on war profiteering while most Serbs sank into poverty.
But others said Ivanic's vote may have been boosted by tens of thousands of Moslem and Croat refugees who thought he would prevent Krajisnik from becoming the chair of the presidency.
The United States called the poll a "major victory for the democratic process" and said it would work with Bosnia's election victors over the next month or so to set up joint governing bodies.
